unit.title: Maintain quality systems within a team

summary: This unit teaches you, as a Level 3 electrician leading a team, to keep your firm's quality system working on every job. You will learn what a quality system contains, how documents, records, test instruments, materials and competence are controlled, and how inspection and test plans, checklists and hold points catch faults early. You will also learn to deal with non-conformances and complaints, find root causes, measure quality with simple figures and charts, take part in audits, and build a team that reports problems and keeps improving.

blocks.p: Quality in electrical work means that the installation meets the client's requirements and the wiring code every time, not only when someone is watching. A firm gets there with a **quality system**: agreed ways of working, checks at the right stages, and records that prove what was done. This unit is for Level 3 electricians who lead a team. You do not write the firm's system, but you are the person who makes it work, or lets it fail, on site each day.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Say what the policy, procedures, work instructions, forms and records are for, and where the job's requirements come from.
Make sure the team works only from current drawings and procedures, and that old copies are withdrawn.
See that test sheets, inspection records, isolation records and certificates are complete, correct, signed and filed.
Follow the inspection and test plan, use checklists, respect hold points, and check work at the right stages.
Use only instruments within calibration, withdraw faulty ones, and check materials when they arrive.
Use training and competence records so that each task is done by someone able to do it.
Make safe, record the non-conformance, correct it, find the root cause and see that it does not come back.
Collect simple figures such as first-time pass rate, defects and rework, and chart them.
Use Plan–Do–Check–Act, team meetings and client feedback to make the work better.
Prepare honestly, answer with evidence and close out findings.

ul: The technical rules come from the wiring code the Centre uses, the makers' instructions and the client's specification. The quality system is how a firm makes sure it meets them.

A new or altered installation must be inspected and certified by a licensed electrical inspector under the **Government Electrical Regulator (GER)** before JPS will connect it. A failed inspection means rework, a second visit and a late handover: quality problems cost time and money.

The best-known standard for quality systems is **ISO 9001**. Some larger clients ask contractors to show that they have a working quality system, and some firms are certified to ISO 9001 by an outside body. A small firm can run a simple system on the same ideas without being certified.
Calibration of test instruments should be done by a laboratory whose measurements can be traced to national or international standards.

blocks.note: The inspector at the end does not make the work good; the people doing it do. Inspection only finds what has already gone wrong. Quality is built in at each step.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Read the sections in order, then try the practice test and read every explanation. Work the percentage examples with a calculator. Your instructor will show you the Centre's own procedures, forms, registers and checklists.
A quality system is the organised way a firm makes sure its work is right: the procedures, checks and records, and the people who use them. Its parts fit together like this.

head: Part
What it is
Electrical example
rows: A short, signed statement of the firm's quality aims
'We install safely, to the code and the client's specification, and we put right what we get wrong.'
'95% of circuits pass inspection first time this year.'
The agreed way an activity is carried out: who does what, and when
Safe isolation; inspection and testing; control of drawings; handling complaints
Terminating an armoured cable; fitting a GFCI outlet; torque settings for a board
Blank documents used to guide and record checks
First-fix checklist; test sheet; isolation record
Completed forms and other evidence of what was done
Signed test sheets, certificates, calibration certificates, training records
Making sure only current, approved documents are in use
Drawing register; revision letters; superseded stamps
Calibration, storage and checks on what is bought
Instrument register; approved suppliers; goods-in checks
Making sure people can do the tasks they are given
Non-conformance reports, corrective and preventive action
A missing earth connection investigated and its cause removed
Audits, measures, client feedback, review meetings
Internal audit of the team's records; monthly defect chart

ul: The **contract, specification and drawings**: what this client wants on this job
The **wiring code** the Centre uses: the technical rules the work must meet
**Makers' instructions**: how each product must be installed, including torque figures
The **firm's own procedures**: how the firm has agreed to work
**Law and the regulator**: safety at work, and inspection before connection

head: Person
Responsibility
rows: Follow the procedures, check their own work, record honestly, report problems
See that procedures and checks are followed each day, that people are competent for their tasks, that records are complete, and that problems are dealt with
Keep the system up to date, run audits, follow up actions
Set the policy, provide people, training and equipment, and review how the system is working

blocks.note: Quality is everyone's job. The team leader does not do every check personally; the team leader makes sure the checks are done, done properly and recorded.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Rework** is doing a job again because it was wrong the first time. It costs labour and materials a second time, delays the handover, may mean another inspection visit, and damages the firm's name. Worst of all, a fault that is not found can injure someone. Getting it right first time is almost always cheaper.
**Worked example.** A job is worth J$1 200 000. Rework on it cost J$84 000. As a percentage of the job's value: 84 000 ÷ 1 200 000 × 100 = **7%**. On many jobs that is most of the profit.

blocks.h: Documents and records are different things

head: Point
Document
Record
rows: An instruction: it says what to do or how
Evidence: it shows what was done and found
Procedure, work instruction, drawing, specification, blank form
Completed and signed test sheet, isolation record, certificate, calibration certificate, audit report
No. A record is never altered, only corrected openly

flow: Each document has a number, a title, a revision and a date
It is approved before it is issued
It is listed on the document register (master list), with who holds copies
A change is proposed, approved and issued as a new revision
Holders get the new revision and are briefed on what changed
Old copies are collected and destroyed, or marked 'superseded'
Users check their copy's revision against the register

ul: The **document register** is the master list showing the current revision of every procedure, form and drawing. If your copy's revision does not match it, your copy is out of date.
A document that has been replaced is **obsolete** or **superseded**. If a copy must be kept for reference, it is clearly marked and kept apart.
Hand-written changes to a procedure in the van are uncontrolled. A better method is **proposed**, approved, written into a new revision, and then briefed to everyone.
Site mark-ups of drawings (red-lines) go back to the office so that the master and the as-built drawings are updated.
Copies on phones and in group chats are uncontrolled: nobody updates them.

blocks.note: Working from an out-of-date drawing or procedure produces work that is neatly done and wrong. Check the revision before you start, not after the inspector points it out.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Filled in **at the time**, by the person who did the work or the test, with the real readings
Complete: job, location, circuit, date, instrument number, result, name and signature
Readable, in ink
Corrected openly: one line through the mistake so that it can still be read, the right entry beside it, initialled and dated. No correction fluid, no writing over figures
Handed in and filed where they can be found, on paper or on a backed-up computer
Kept for the time the firm's procedure sets, often several years after the job

blocks.p: Records are kept because the firm may need to prove, long after the job, that the work was checked: to a client, an insurer, the regulator or a court. They also let the firm trace which jobs an instrument, a batch of material or a person worked on if a problem appears later. **Worked example:** if the procedure says test sheets are kept for 6 years and a job is finished in 2026, its sheets are kept until 2032.

blocks.note: Never write up a record you did not make at the time, and never sign for a test you did not do or see. A false record is worse than a missing one: it hides a danger and destroys trust in every other record.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: At the end of a job the client receives the documents that show the installation is safe and what it contains: the certificate and test results, the board schedules, the as-built drawings, and the makers' instructions and warranties. The **certificate** tells the client in writing that the installation was inspected and tested and the results were satisfactory.

An inspection and test plan (ITP), or quality plan, sets out for one job **what is checked, at which stage, by whom, against what standard, and what record is made**. The team leader receives it before the job starts and plans the work round it.

head: Stage
Check
By
Accept if
Record
rows: Routes, box positions and heights, supports, bushings, conduit ends
Terminations, tightness to the maker's torque, polarity, labels
Electrician, then a second person on main connections
Continuity of protective conductors, insulation resistance, polarity
Within the limits in the procedure
GFCI or RCD operation, voltage, operation of equipment
Within the limits in the procedure

ul: A **hold point** is a stage where work must stop until a named person has inspected and signed. The usual one for electricians is first fix, before walls and ceilings are closed: after that, a fault can only be reached by breaking the finish.
A **witness point** is a stage the client or inspector has asked to see, such as a test. They are told in advance; if they do not attend, the work may go on as the plan allows.

head: Check
Who
Why
rows: The person who did the work, before passing it on
The cheapest place to find a fault is where it was made
A colleague, on critical items such as the main earth, main connections and labelling
A second pair of eyes catches what the first missed
The team leader, at agreed stages and by sampling
Confirms that the checks are being done and the standard is steady
The firm's inspector, the client's engineer, the GER inspector
An outside view before the work is accepted

blocks.p: A checklist turns 'I think I checked everything' into evidence. Using the **same checklist for every board** means nothing is forgotten, results can be compared between jobs and people, and a new item can be added for everyone when a problem is found. Each line should say what to look for and, where it applies, the limit that passes.

blocks.note: Tighten terminals with a torque screwdriver set to the maker's figure, and mark each one as it is done if the firm's procedure asks for it. A loose terminal overheats; an over-tightened one can crack or damage the conductor. Neither can be seen once the cover is on.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Test results are only as good as the instrument. An insulation tester that reads high could pass a circuit with damaged insulation.

head: Control
What it means
rows: Each instrument has its own number, marked on it
A list of every instrument with its type, serial number, who holds it, the date of its last calibration and the date the next is due
Comparison against a more accurate standard by a competent laboratory, at a set **calibration interval** (often 12 months; the firm's procedure says)
The label on the instrument shows the due date; the certificate is filed as a record
Before use: label in date, case and leads undamaged, battery good, leads nulled on a low-resistance ohmmeter, voltage indicator proved on a proving unit before and after
Carried in its case, kept dry, not left in a hot van or dropped

blocks.h: When an instrument is faulty or out of calibration

flow: Stop using it at once
Tag it 'OUT OF SERVICE' and keep it apart from good instruments
Tell the team leader; record it
Find every job it was used on since its last good check, from the instrument numbers on the test sheets
Review those results; retest where the error could have changed a pass to a fail
Repair and recalibrate it; check the new certificate and update the register before it is used again

blocks.p: Results that were close to the pass limit need the closest look. If a tester was reading 20% high, a recorded 1.1 MΩ may really have been about 0.9 MΩ. Results far above the limit are less likely to be affected, but the procedure decides what is retested.

blocks.note: This is why every test sheet carries the instrument's number. Without it, nobody can tell which jobs a faulty instrument was used on, and every job would have to be retested.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Buy from **approved suppliers**: ones the firm has checked and had good results from.
Check deliveries **on arrival**, not after fitting: the right type, rating and size, the maker's markings and certification marks, the quantity against the delivery note, and no damage.
Be alert for **fake or sub-standard** breakers, cable and accessories: missing or misspelt markings, unusually light weight, a price far below normal. Do not fit anything you doubt.
Label non-conforming material, keep it apart so nobody uses it, and report it.
Store materials dry and off the ground, with cable drums protected from sun and damage.

blocks.p: **Competence** is the proven ability to do a task to the required standard: training plus assessed practice. The firm keeps a record of what each person has been trained and assessed to do, often as a **competence matrix**.

ul: The team leader uses the matrix to give each task to someone competent, and to pair learners with experienced people.
It shows the gaps, so training can be planned.
When a fault is traced to a lack of skill, the record shows who else may need the same training.
Clients and auditors can see that the team is qualified for the work.

sections.title: Dealing with problems: non-conformance and corrective action

blocks.p: A **non-conformance** is anything that does not meet a requirement: work, material, a document or a record. Finding one is not a disgrace. Hiding one is.

flow: Make it safe: isolate, lock off and tag if there is any danger; tell the client what not to use
Record it on a non-conformance report (NCR)
Contain it: check whether the same fault exists elsewhere
Correct it, and re-inspect or retest
Find the root cause
Take corrective action to remove the cause
Check later that the action has worked, then close the report

ul: What was found, where and when, and who found it, with a photo if possible
The requirement it fails (drawing, code, procedure, maker's instruction)
What was done at once to make it safe and to correct it
The root cause
The corrective action, who will do it and by when
Evidence that the action worked, and the sign-off that closes the report

head: Action
What it does
Example
rows: Fixes the fault that was found. It does not ask why it happened.
A cover plate is found cracked at inspection and is replaced.
Finds and removes the **cause** of a problem that has happened, so that it does not happen again.
Cover plates keep cracking. The cause is traced to screws driven with an impact driver, so the team is issued with hand screwdrivers for accessories and the work instruction is changed.
Removes the cause of a problem that has **not yet** happened but could.
Before a job with a new type of board, the team practises on a sample and adds the maker's torque figures to the checklist.

blocks.p: A correction is needed straight away, but a correction alone means the fault will be back on the next job. A report is **closed** only when the fix has been checked and the corrective action has been shown to work, not when the form has been filled in.

One fault found usually means others like it. If one outlet has no earth connection, test every outlet the team wired on that job, and think about other recent jobs by the same people using the same method. If a tool or instrument was at fault, look at everything it was used on.

ul: Log every complaint, however small, with the date, the client's words and who took it.
Respond quickly: make safe first, then investigate and correct.
Treat it as a non-conformance: find the cause and prevent others.
Tell the client what was found and what has been done.
Ask clients for feedback at handover, good and bad, and review it at team meetings. Praise shows what to keep doing; complaints show what to change.

blocks.note: A missing or loose protective (earth) conductor, reversed polarity, or a circuit left without its GFCI protection is a danger to life, not a paperwork matter. Isolate first; write afterwards.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The **root cause** is the deepest reason a problem happened: the thing that, if changed, stops it coming back. 'The electrician forgot' is rarely a root cause. Ask why forgetting was possible, and why nothing caught it.
Ask 'why?' again and again, usually about five times, until you reach something in the system that can be changed.

head: Question
Answer
rows: Why did the water heater circuit fail the insulation test?
The cable's insulation was cut at the conduit entry to the heater's isolator.
The conduit end was sharp and had no bushing.
There were none on the van that day.
Why were there none on the van?
Bushings are not on the van's stock list, so nobody restocks them.
Why are they not on the list?
The list was written before the firm changed to this conduit system and was never reviewed.

blocks.p: Root cause: the van stock list is out of date and is not reviewed. Corrective action: add bushings with a minimum quantity, check van stock weekly, and add 'bushing fitted' to the first-fix checklist. Telling the electrician to be more careful would change nothing.

When a problem may have several causes, a fishbone diagram helps the team sort them. The problem is written at the 'head'; each 'bone' is a group of possible causes. The team suggests causes under each group, then checks which ones the facts support.

head: Group
Questions to ask
Example for 'boards failing inspection for labelling'
rows: New members never shown the firm's label format
Labels written at the very end, in a hurry
Label sheets not supplied with the boards
Label printer left at the office
No line for labels on the checklist
Heat, light, space, weather, time pressure
Poor light in the switch cupboard at the end of the day

blocks.note: Look for causes in the system before you look for someone to blame. If one person made a mistake, others can make it too, unless the method, the tools or the checks change.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **key performance indicator (KPI)** is a figure that shows how well something is going. Measures turn opinions into facts, and they come from records the team already keeps.

head: Measure
How it is worked out
Source
rows: Items passing inspection first time ÷ items inspected × 100
A tally of each kind of defect
Hours and materials spent on rework; rework cost ÷ job value × 100
Number per month or per job, and time taken to close them
Jobs with a full, signed handover file ÷ jobs finished × 100
Number past their calibration date (the target is none)

blocks.p: **Worked examples.** 66 of 75 circuits pass first time: 66 ÷ 75 × 100 = **88%**. 3 boards out of 60 need rework: 3 ÷ 60 × 100 = **5%**. Defects fall from 24 one month to 18 the next: the fall is 6, and 6 ÷ 24 × 100 = **25%** (always divide by the starting figure). 27 of 36 clients rate the service 'good': 27 ÷ 36 × 100 = **75%**.

A **Pareto chart** is a bar chart of problems in order from the most frequent to the least. It usually shows that a few kinds of defect make up most of the total, so the team knows where to put its effort first.

Here two of the five types make up 77% of the 30 defects. Fixing labelling and torque first will do far more than spreading effort over everything. To see whether a change worked, compare the same count **before and after** it.

head: Step
What the team does
rows: Collect the facts, find the likely cause, plan a change and set a target
Try the change, usually on a small scale first, and train the people involved
Measure the results and compare them with the target and with before
If it worked, make it the standard: update the procedure and brief everyone. If not, learn from it and plan again

blocks.p: The cycle then starts again on the next problem. This steady, small-step improvement, with everyone involved, is called **continuous improvement**; some firms use the Japanese word **kaizen**. It is the opposite of both 'we have always done it this way' and of changing methods without telling anyone or dropping checks to save time.

A short weekly meeting, 10 to 15 minutes, keeps quality in view: last week's defects and their causes, the chart, actions agreed and whether earlier actions worked, any complaints or praise, and ideas from the team. It is not for naming who made the most mistakes.

An **audit** is a planned check that the system is being followed and is working. An **internal audit** is done by the firm's own trained people; an external audit by a client or a certification body. An audit checks the system, not individuals, by comparing what the procedures say with what the auditor sees and what the records show.

head: Finding
Meaning
rows: A requirement is not being met. A major one means a serious or repeated failure.
Not yet a failure, but a weakness that could become one
A suggestion; the system meets the requirement but could be better

ul: **Before**: check that documents are current, records complete and signed, instruments in date and labelled, and that everyone knows where the procedures are. Do not create or back-date records.
**During**: answer honestly, show the real records and explain what you actually do. If you do not know, say so and show where the answer is kept.
**After**: for each finding, correct it, find the root cause, agree an action with an owner and a date, do it, and give the auditor the evidence so the finding can be closed.
Thank people who report their own mistakes and near misses: a fault found early is cheap to fix.
Never shout at or shame someone in front of others. People who are punished for honesty stop being honest.
Explain why each check matters, not only that it must be done.
Share the results, good and bad, and praise good work.
Follow the system yourself. The team copies what the leader does, not what the leader says.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain what a quality system is and name its main parts.
I can tell a policy from a procedure, a work instruction, a form and a record.
I can say where a job's quality requirements come from.
I can check that a document is current against the register, and deal with a superseded copy.
I can say what makes a good record, and correct an entry properly.
I can follow an inspection and test plan and explain hold points and witness points.
I can explain self-inspection, second-person checks and why the same checklist is used every time.
I can check an instrument before use and say what to do when one is faulty or out of calibration.
I can check materials on arrival and deal with doubtful items.
I can use a competence matrix to give out tasks.
I can raise a non-conformance report and tell correction, corrective action and preventive action apart.
I can find a root cause with the 5 whys or a fishbone diagram.
I can work out pass rates, rework percentages and percentage changes, and read a Pareto chart.
I can run an improvement with Plan–Do–Check–Act.
I can prepare for an audit honestly and close out its findings.
I can lead a team in a way that makes people willing to report problems.

terms: Audit
A planned check that the quality system is being followed and is working.
Calibration
Comparing an instrument with a more accurate standard to confirm that it reads correctly.
Calibration interval
The set period between one calibration and the next.
Competence
Proven ability to do a task to the required standard.
Containment
Checking for, and holding, other items that may have the same fault.
Continuous improvement (kaizen)
Steady, small-step improvement of the way work is done.
Correction
Fixing a fault that has been found.
Corrective action
Removing the cause of a problem that has happened, so that it does not happen again.
Document register
The master list showing the current revision of every controlled document.
First-time pass rate
The percentage of items that pass inspection without rework.
Fishbone diagram
A cause-and-effect diagram that sorts the possible causes of a problem into groups.
5 whys
Asking 'why?' repeatedly to reach the root cause of a problem.
Hold point
A stage where work must stop until it has been inspected and signed off.
Inspection and test plan (ITP)
A plan of what is checked, when, by whom, against what, and what record is made.
KPI
Key performance indicator: a figure that shows how well something is going.
Non-conformance report (NCR)
The form that records something that does not meet a requirement and what is done about it.
Obsolete (superseded)
Withdrawn and replaced by a newer revision.
Pareto chart
A bar chart of problems in order from the most to the least frequent.
Plan–Do–Check–Act
A four-step cycle for making and testing an improvement.
Preventive action
Removing the cause of a problem that could happen but has not yet.
Procedure
The agreed way of carrying out an activity.
Quality policy
A short, signed statement of the firm's quality aims.
Record
Evidence of what was done or found, such as a signed test sheet.
Rework
Doing work again because it was not right the first time.
Root cause
The deepest reason a problem happened.
Self-inspection
The checks a worker makes on their own work before passing it on.
Work instruction
Step-by-step detail of how to do one task.

c1.title: First-fix defects at a housing scheme near Longville Park
c1.text: Carlton Reid's team is first-fixing 60 houses at a housing scheme near Longville Park, Clarendon. The firm's inspection and test plan has a hold point at first fix. The firm's inspector has recorded 26 defects this month: 14 conduit ends without bushings, 6 cables not supported, 3 boxes out of level, 2 boxes at the wrong height and 1 damaged conduit. Asking 'why' shows that bushings are often missing from the vans.

c2.title: A tester past its date in Duncans
c2.text: At a contractor in Duncans, Trelawny, a monthly check finds that multifunction tester MFT-04 is seven weeks past its calibration date. In those weeks it was used to test nine jobs. It is sent to a calibration laboratory, which reports that its insulation resistance range was reading about 30% high and adjusts it. Every test sheet in the firm records the instrument's number.

c3.title: A complaint from a dental office in Liguanea
c3.text: Three weeks after Ms Clarke's team rewired a dental office in Liguanea, St Andrew, the dentist complains that the lights in two surgeries flicker when the compressor starts. An electrician isolates the sub-board, finds a loose neutral connection and tightens it. Ms Clarke then learns that the team's torque screwdriver went missing before that job, and that the second-fix checklist has no line for neutral-bar connections.

c4.title: Getting ready for an audit in Santa Cruz
c4.text: The firm's quality officer will audit Delano Williams's team next Tuesday at a supermarket job in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. Preparing for it, Delano finds that the site copy of the safe isolation procedure is revision 2, although the document register shows revision 3. He also finds that Rushane, who joined last month, has been dead-testing circuits alone, although the competence matrix shows him as 'not yet' for testing.

c5.title: Fewer failed insulation tests in Mandeville
c5.text: Over two months, 9 of the 60 circuits that Jodi-Ann Spence's team tested in new houses in Mandeville, Manchester, failed the insulation resistance test the first time. Each time, the cable's insulation had been scraped while it was pulled through conduit. The team agrees to try a new method on the next ten houses: deburr every conduit end, fit bushings, use pulling lubricant and have a second person feed the cable. In those ten houses, 1 of 50 circuits fails first time.

questions.q: What share of the month's defects do the two most common types make up?
o: About 23%
About 77%
About 54%
About 88%
questions.why: Missing bushings (14) and unsupported cables (6) make 20 of the 26 defects: 20 ÷ 26 × 100 is about 77%. This is what a Pareto chart shows: fixing two types of defect would remove most of the problem.

questions.q: Why is a conduit end without a bushing a real quality problem, and not just untidy work?
o: The inspector cannot see into the conduit
The conduit can fill with water at that end
The sharp edge can cut the cable's insulation
The conduit will rust faster without a bushing
questions.why: A raw conduit end is sharp. It can scrape or cut insulation as cables are pulled in, or later as they move, leaving a fault that may show only as a failed insulation test, a shock or a fire.

questions.q: Which corrective action deals best with the cause Carlton has found?
o: Fit bushings only in the houses the inspector will visit
Add bushings to the van stock list, with weekly checks
Take the bushing line off the first-fix checklist
Tell the electricians to take more care with conduit ends
questions.why: The cause is that bushings are often not on the vans, so the action must change the system: put them on the stock list with a minimum quantity and check it. Asking people to take more care does not put bushings on the van.

questions.q: The plastering contractor wants to start on house 12 before the first fix has been inspected. What does the hold point mean here?
o: Plastering may start if Carlton has looked at the house himself
Plastering waits until the first fix is inspected and signed
Plastering may start, and any faults can be fixed afterwards
Plastering waits until all 60 houses have been first-fixed
questions.why: A hold point stops the work at that stage until the named person has inspected and signed. After plastering, a fault can only be reached by breaking the finish, so the check must come first. It applies house by house, not to the whole scheme.

questions.q: Why is an insulation tester that reads 30% high a safety concern?
o: It could fail insulation that is really sound
It could damage cables by testing at too high a voltage
It could give the person using it an electric shock
It could pass insulation that should have failed
questions.why: If the tester shows more resistance than is really there, a circuit with weak or damaged insulation can appear to pass. A tester that read low would cause needless rework, but one that reads high hides danger.

questions.q: Which of the nine jobs' results need the closest look?
o: Those with readings only just above the pass limit
None, since every circuit passed when it was tested
Those tested most recently, as errors grow with time
Those on the largest and most costly jobs
questions.why: A reading 30% high matters most where the recorded figure was only a little above the limit: the true value may have been below it. Those circuits must be retested. Readings far above the limit would still pass after allowing for the error, though the procedure decides.

questions.q: How can the firm find which circuits were tested with MFT-04 in those seven weeks?
o: Ask each electrician what they remember using
Retest every job done by the firm this year
Check which jobs had complaints from clients
Use the instrument numbers on the test sheets
questions.why: Each test sheet records the number of the instrument used, so the affected jobs can be traced exactly. Without that, the firm would have to rely on memory or retest everything.

questions.q: Which change would best stop an instrument going past its date again?
o: Check calibration dates when an audit is announced
Ask each user to remember their instrument's date
Buy a new tester every year and scrap the old ones
Review the register monthly and book ahead
questions.why: A register only works if someone looks at it. A monthly review, with each instrument booked in before its due date, makes the system catch the date, not individual memory. Users still check the label before each use.

questions.q: The electrician tightened the loose neutral. What kind of action is that?
o: A preventive action
A corrective action
A correction
An audit finding
questions.why: Tightening the connection fixes the fault that was found, which is a correction. It does not deal with why the connection was loose, so on its own it will not stop the same fault on the next job.

questions.q: Which action deals with the cause of the loose neutral?
o: Remind the team at the next briefing to tighten things well
Ask the dentist to report at once if the lights flicker again
Tighten every connection in the dental office a little harder
Replace the torque tool and add neutrals to the checklist
questions.why: Two things let the fault through: no torque tool, and no check of neutral-bar connections. Corrective action removes both. A reminder changes nothing in the system, and 'a little harder' without a torque tool risks damage.

questions.q: What should Ms Clarke do about the team's other recent jobs?
o: Check the boards done without the torque tool
Retest the insulation resistance of every circuit wired
Send each client a letter of apology in advance
Nothing, unless another client makes a similar complaint
questions.why: The same cause was present on every board the team terminated without the torque screwdriver, so those boards may have loose connections too. Containment means looking for the fault wherever its cause existed, before it shows itself.

questions.q: What should Delano do about the revision 2 isolation procedure on site?
o: Write the changes on it by hand from memory
Keep it, since the steps are nearly the same
Replace it with revision 3 and brief the team
Hide it until the audit is over, then bring it back
questions.why: The register shows revision 3 is current, so the site copy is superseded. Replace it, remove the old copy, and brief the team on what changed, because they have been working to the old steps. Hand-written changes are uncontrolled.

questions.q: What should Delano do about Rushane's testing?
o: Let him carry on, as his results have all been passes
Mark him as 'assessed' on the matrix before the audit
Stop him testing alone and have his results checked
Move him to another site until the audit is finished
questions.why: Rushane has not been assessed as competent to test, so his results cannot be relied on. He should test only under supervision until he is assessed, and the circuits he tested should be checked. Changing the matrix without an assessment would be a false record.

questions.q: During the audit, Delano is asked how the firm handles client complaints, and he is not sure. What is his best answer?
o: Say he is unsure, and show where the procedure is
Tell the auditor that complaints are not his team's job
Describe what he thinks the procedure probably says
Change the subject to the team's good test records
questions.why: An audit looks for evidence of what really happens. Saying honestly that he is unsure, and showing where to find the procedure, is better than a guess that may be wrong. The gap can then be closed by a briefing.

questions.q: The auditor finds the team's isolation records complete, but suggests a clearer layout for the form. What kind of finding is this?
o: A major non-conformity
A minor non-conformity
An opportunity for improvement
A corrective action for the whole firm
questions.why: The requirement is being met, so it is not a non-conformity. A suggestion that would make a working system better is an opportunity for improvement; the firm decides whether to adopt it through its document control.

questions.q: What was the first-test failure rate before the new method?
questions.why: 9 failures out of 60 circuits: 9 ÷ 60 × 100 = 15%. This starting figure is needed so that the result of the trial can be compared with it.

questions.q: Trying the new method on the next ten houses is which step of Plan–Do–Check–Act?
o: Check
Do
Act
Plan
questions.why: Plan was collecting the facts, finding the cause and agreeing the change. Do is trying the change, usually on a small scale. Counting the failures afterwards is Check, and making the method standard is Act.

questions.q: After the trial, what should the team do next?
o: Make it standard: update the work instruction and brief all
Keep using it quietly within the team that ran the trial
Go back to the old method, since one circuit still failed
Stop testing insulation, as nearly every circuit now passes
questions.why: Failures fell from 15% to 2% (1 in 50), so the change worked. The Act step makes it the standard way of working through document control, so every team gains. Testing continues: it is how the team knows the method still works.

questions.q: A signed isolation record and the safe isolation procedure are both in the job file. How do they differ?
o: The record says how to do it; the procedure shows it was done
The procedure is for trainees; the record is for electricians
They do not differ: both are records of the same activity
The procedure says how to do it; the record shows it was done
questions.why: A procedure is an instruction that can be revised under document control. A record is evidence of what was actually done, when and by whom, and it is never altered afterwards.

questions.q: You notice that you wrote a wrong reading on a test sheet an hour ago. How should you correct it?
o: Cover it with correction fluid and write the right figure in
Strike it through once, add the right figure, initial it
Write the right figure over the wrong one in heavier ink
Throw the sheet away and fill in a clean one from memory
questions.why: A record must show its history. One line through the error keeps it readable, and the initials and date show who corrected it and when. Hidden changes or rewritten sheets make a record impossible to trust.
